title: Mardana and the rebab
hookLine: a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, becomes his lifelong companion; Mardana plays and Nanak sings
last: WHERE IS YOUR MIND RIGHT NOW?

cards: Guru Nanak had a partner, the player whose hands made the song work. His name was Mardana. He came from Nanak's own village, Talwandi, and tradition says he was about ten years older.
He was a Muslim, from a family of hereditary musicians, the kind who played at weddings and sang the genealogies of the village. And he carried an instrument everywhere he went.
When Nanak came out of the river with something to say, Mardana gave it a tune.

teach.b: The instrument was a rebab: plucked strings, a wooden body, skin stretched across the front, and a deep, woody voice. It's the ancestor, or at least a cousin, of instruments played across Central and South Asia today.
Here's how the two of them worked.

teach.h: MARDANA, PLAY. THE WORD IS COMING.
teach.b: Nanak would feel a hymn coming, and tradition says he'd turn to his friend with something like: Mardana, play the rebab, the Word is coming. Mardana found the note, and Nanak sang.
So Sikh scripture didn't begin as something read silently.

It was born as music. That's why the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga, by musical mode, and why, in a gurdwara today, the hymns are still sung to instruments. Now look at who's holding the rebab.

teach.h: A MUSLIM MUSICIAN AT NANAK'S SIDE.
teach.b: A Muslim musician sat at the side of a teacher born into a Hindu family, and for years they walked together, ate together and slept on the same roads.
There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim: Mardana is that line with a face and a pair of hands. Sikhs still honor him by name.
A few verses in the scripture carry his name, and, tradition says, his descendants, the rababis, sang the hymns in Sikh gatherings for generations.
Neither of them did it alone. The words needed the music, and the music needed the words. With this, the early years close: the boy at Talwandi, the river, the storehouse, the first words after.

how: Sikh hymns are sung, not only read: in gurdwaras, musicians called ragis sing the scripture to instruments in the ragas it is arranged by, and Bhai Mardana is remembered as the Guru's own musician.

games.q: you're Nanak. a hymn is rising in you, and your friend is sitting beside you with his rebab. what do you do?
o: write it down quietly for later.
ask Mardana to play, and sing it.
wait until you find a temple.
games.why: tradition says he'd turn to Mardana and ask him to play, because the Word was coming. the hymns were born as songs.

practice: Put on one piece of music, any music, or let the bell's two minutes be the music, and listen all the way through, doing nothing else; stay even through the part you usually skip.
Listen for the instrument underneath the voice, the one you normally don't hear. Somebody is playing it, so the singer can sing.

wordCard.voice: Rebab. The stringed instrument Bhai Mardana played beside Guru Nanak, so the hymns could be sung. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the rebab, the string instrument of Bhai Mardana; the word came into Punjabi from Persian and Arabic.

carryVoice: Your line: one plays, one sings. Tomorrow the two of them walk out of town. Day thirty-one.
